title: Understanding Brazil's 2026 presidential runoff
lede: Who won, how Brazil's two-round system works, and what a fourth Lula term means at home and in a world of US tariffs and shifting blocs. Based on Superior Electoral Court (TSE) figures, as of 10 November 2026.

stats.l: Lula's share of valid votes in the runoff

visual.label: Runoff share of valid votes: Lula 51.79%, Flávio Bolsonaro 48.21%

visual_note: Lula, of the Workers' Party (PT), finished second in the first round on 4 October (Flávio 47.03%, Lula 45.16%) and won the runoff, the first candidate to do so since two rounds began in 1989. The map counts votes cast in Brazil's states; overseas votes are part of the national total only.

cells: Liberal Party (PL), right; senator and son of Jair Bolsonaro

table.note: Shares of valid votes. Third in the first round was Augusto Cury (Avante) with 2.89%.

elects: The president of Brazil, for a four-year term starting 5 January 2027. This page maps the runoff. The same general election also chose governors, the federal Congress and state legislatures, and that Congress is the other half of the story.
Lula, 80, takes a fourth non-consecutive term and has said it will be his last. His opponent was Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, whose father Jair Bolsonaro was president from 2019 to 2022.

system.oneline: A candidate needs more than half of valid votes. If nobody gets there, the top two go to a runoff three weeks later.

steps.p: Voting is compulsory for citizens aged 18 to 70 and optional for 16 to 17 and over 70. Brazil votes on electronic machines and the TSE counts nationally, usually finishing within hours.
Blank and spoiled ballots do not count. A first-round winner needs an absolute majority of the rest; in 2026 nobody got there.

steps.h: The runoff is a straight choice
steps.p: The top two candidates meet again on the last Sunday of October. Whoever has more votes wins, by any margin.

There is no Electoral College. Every vote counts the same wherever it is cast, so São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Rio de Janeiro, with the most voters, matter most. That is why the Electorate map view looks so different from the land view.

home: The margin was thin, about 4.4 million votes, and the reaction was not calm. Flávio Bolsonaro rejected the result and asked for it to be annulled. The TSE president said an extension of voting time had not affected the outcome, and legal experts questioned whether there were grounds to overturn it.

home.h: A reversal of the first round
home.p: The first round favoured Flávio Bolsonaro. Lula closed the gap in the runoff. His strongest states were in the north-east, as the Electorate map shows, and his campaign leaned on defending national sovereignty against US pressure.
Reporting expects resistance in the Senate to his judicial and institutional appointments. Winning the presidency does not by itself settle whether he has a working majority in Congress.

world.p: Washington imposed a 50% tariff on many Brazilian exports in 2025, citing among other things Bolsonaro's prosecution and trade practices. Two further rounds of tariffs followed in July 2026. Lula campaigned on resisting them. After the win, the EU, Mexico, India, France, Canada and Russia congratulated him, while the United States was initially silent.

Brazil has answered US pressure by pushing the EU–Mercosur trade agreement and coordinating with BRICS partners, a strategy analysts describe as avoiding a choice between the US and China. A fourth Lula term means that approach continues.

Trump-aligned governments have won elsewhere in Latin America, which could weaken Brazil's bargaining position with Washington. The Bolsonaro family has also campaigned in the US for the former president, and Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly headed to the United States after the vote.

p: A Bolsonaro win would have been the first return of the family's movement to power after Jair Bolsonaro's 2022 defeat. The likeliest first effect abroad would have been a thaw with Washington, including pressure on the tariff dispute, and Brazil sitting closer to the region's Trump-aligned governments.
At home it would have reversed the direction of the social and environmental policy that Lula's coalition champions. With Lula re-elected, the EU–Mercosur and BRICS routes stay open.
